title: Schema and data types
note: missing columns: none; unexpected: none; CustomerID dtype = float64
impact: CustomerID is stored as a float (17850.0) and InvoiceNo/StockCode mix numbers and text. Joining to a CRM or product master on these keys can silently fail ('17850' != '17850.0'), and Excel round-trips can strip letter suffixes or leading zeros, merging distinct products.

title: Missing CustomerID
note: median UnitPrice is 3.29 on rows without CustomerID vs 1.95 with one, so these rows are not a random sample
impact: About a quarter of lines have no customer. Customer counts, RFM, CLV, retention and cohort analyses are computed on a biased subset (guest / walk-in / manual orders behave differently). If these rows are dropped for customer work but kept for revenue, the two views will not reconcile.

title: Missing or blank Description
note: 1,454 of these have UnitPrice = 0 and 1,454 have no CustomerID
impact: Lines without a description cannot be named in product reports and are mostly zero-price stock adjustments, not sales. Grouping by Description would create an 'NaN' product; grouping by StockCode keeps them but mixes adjustments into the product's unit history.

title: Exact duplicate rows (all 8 fields identical)
impact: Identical lines inflate revenue, units and order frequency. They may be legitimate (same item scanned twice on one invoice) or an extract/ETL duplication — the data cannot tell you which, so confirm with the source system before removing. Only the 2nd+ occurrence is flagged.

title: Cancellation invoices (InvoiceNo starts with 'C')
impact: Cancellations carry negative quantities. Summing all lines gives net revenue; filtering Quantity > 0 gives gross sales but leaves cancelled orders counted as sales. Either way, treat returns explicitly: they lower product sell-through, can make a customer look more or less valuable, and inflate order counts if cancellation invoices are counted as orders.

title: Negative quantity on a non-cancellation invoice
impact: These are usually warehouse write-offs (damaged, lost, 'wet') entered as sales lines, typically at price 0 and with no customer. They don't move revenue much but they reduce unit volumes and can make a product look like it sold less, or even net negative in a month.

title: Positive quantity on a cancellation invoice
impact: A cancellation that adds units contradicts the invoice type and would double-count revenue if cancellations are netted by sign.

title: Cancellation with no earlier matching purchase in file
impact: The original sale is likely before the data window starts. Netting these against in-window sales understates revenue for the first months and can make a customer's net spend negative. Heuristic match on CustomerID + StockCode + earlier date; non-product codes (e.g. 'D' discounts) are included here and also flagged separately.

title: UnitPrice = 0
impact: Zero-price lines are free samples, adjustments or data-entry gaps. They add units with no revenue, pulling average selling price down and inflating product 'popularity' and basket-size metrics.

title: UnitPrice < 0
impact: Negative prices are accounting entries (e.g. 'Adjust bad debt'), not sales. A single line can move monthly revenue by thousands.

title: Non-merchandise StockCode (postage, fees, manual, discounts)
impact: POST, DOT, M (Manual), D (Discount), BANK CHARGES, AMAZONFEE, CRUK etc. are not products. Left in, POSTAGE/DOTCOM POSTAGE rank among the 'top products'; Manual and AMAZONFEE lines contain the largest single values in the file and swing monthly revenue; per-product price and margin analysis becomes meaningless for these codes.

title: Description looks like a stock note (damaged, lost, '?')
impact: Warehouse notes typed into Description ('damaged', 'wet pallet', '?') create fake product names and distort unit volumes for the real StockCode. Filter on (price = 0 or qty < 0) to avoid matching genuine products whose name contains a keyword.

title: Extreme line (abs Quantity >= 10,000 or abs UnitPrice >= 5,000)
impact: A handful of lines (e.g. 80,995 units of one item, cancelled minutes later) dominate totals: they create a fake revenue spike in one month, make one customer the 'top customer', and make a cheap item the 'best seller' unless the matching cancellation is also netted.

title: Quantity > 50x the product's median order size (and >= 100 units)
impact: Unusually large orders relative to the product's normal order size are often wholesale orders; they are real but skew mean order size, forecasting and customer segmentation. Review before excluding.

title: UnitPrice > 5x or < 1/5 of the product's median price
impact: A price far from the product's usual price suggests a keying error, a pack-vs-unit mismatch or a manual override. Average selling price and price-elasticity estimates are sensitive to these.

title: StockCode with more than one Description
impact: Product reports grouped by Description split one product into several rows (and merge different products sharing a name, below). Pick one canonical key — StockCode — and a rule for the display name.

title: Description shared by more than one StockCode
impact: The same name on several codes (colour/size variants or re-coded items) means a Description-level report merges distinct SKUs, while a StockCode-level report splits what the business may consider one product.

title: StockCode differs only by letter case (lowercase variant flagged)
impact: Codes like '85123a' and '85123A' are counted as two products in any case-sensitive groupby, splitting sales and stock history.

title: Description with leading/trailing/double spaces
note: 113,452 have trailing/leading spaces (harmless unless names are joined to another table); 22,290 contain double spaces
impact: Whitespace variants of the same name group separately, inflating the product count and splitting volumes.

title: Product with max/min unit price ratio > 10
impact: Large price spread for one SKU usually signals mixed units of sale (single vs pack), wholesale vs retail pricing, or entry errors. Revenue is still 'right' line by line, but average price, price-mix and revenue-per-unit comparisons across products are not.

title: Invoice linked to more than one CustomerID (incl. missing)
impact: An invoice should belong to one customer. Mixed IDs mean revenue for that order is split across customers in CLV/RFM.

title: Invoice with more than one InvoiceDate
impact: Lines of one order carry different timestamps; daily/hourly sales and order-level date logic (first purchase, recency) depend on which line you pick.

title: Invoice with more than one Country
impact: Country revenue splits a single order across markets.

title: Same StockCode on multiple lines of one invoice (not exact duplicate)
impact: Split lines (different qty or price) are usually legitimate, but they inflate 'line count' / 'items per basket' metrics and complicate matching cancellations back to the original line.

title: CustomerID appearing with more than one Country
impact: A customer assigned to several countries is double-counted in country-level customer counts and their revenue is split across markets.

title: Customer with negative net revenue over the whole file
impact: Usually customers whose original purchases pre-date the file (see orphan cancellations). They break CLV models that assume non-negative spend and distort segment averages.

title: Country is 'Unspecified' or 'European Community'
impact: These are not countries; geographic revenue and customer counts will have an unassignable bucket. Also note 'EIRE' (Ireland) and 'RSA' (South Africa) use non-standard names that won't join to ISO country lists.

title: Partial first/last month and calendar gaps
note: 69 calendar days with no transactions; weekday counts: {'Thursday': 103857, 'Tuesday': 101808, 'Monday': 95111, 'Wednesday': 94565, 'Friday': 82193, 'Sunday': 64375}
impact: Data runs 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09. The last month (2011-12) has only 8 trading days, so a naive monthly chart shows a collapse that isn't real; MoM/YoY and customer churn ('no purchase in last 30 days') are biased at the end. Only one December appears in full, so seasonality cannot be estimated from a single cycle. There are no Saturday transactions at all, and the Christmas/New Year shutdown leaves a multi-week gap; both matter for daily averages and day-of-week analysis.
